reference.source: ISSVA classification / Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant primary lymphoedema caused by loss-of-function variants in FOXC2
The two defining features are lower-limb lymphoedema and distichiasis, an accessory row of eyelashes arising from the meibomian gland openings
Lymphoedema characteristically appears later than in Milroy disease, typically around puberty or in early adulthood, and predominantly affects the legs
Distichiasis may cause ocular irritation, corneal changes and photophobia, and can be present from birth even before oedema develops
Associated features include varicose veins (often of early onset), ptosis, cleft palate and, importantly, congenital heart disease
Unlike Milroy disease, the lymphatic defect is thought to involve lymphatic valve dysfunction and reflux rather than simple hypoplasia
Diagnosis combines the clinical dyad with family history and FOXC2 genetic testing, supported by lymphoscintigraphy
Management is supportive lymphoedema care with compression and skin care, ophthalmic treatment of distichiasis, and cardiac evaluation
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphoedema-distichiasis syndrome is an autosomal dominant primary lymphatic disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in the transcription factor FOXC2, which is essential for normal development of lymphatic valves and vessels. The resulting valvular dysfunction leads to lymphatic reflux and impaired drainage, producing lower-limb lymphoedema, and the same developmental disturbance affects venous valves (accounting for varicose veins) and eyelash follicles (distichiasis). FOXC2 also contributes to eyelid, palatal and cardiac development, explaining the associated anomalies.
additionalDifferentials: Milroy disease (congenital VEGFR3-related lymphoedema without distichiasis)
Systemic causes of leg oedema (cardiac, renal, hepatic)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to confirm distichiasis and assess corneal effects
Lymphoscintigraphy to characterise lymphatic drainage and reflux
Echocardiography to screen for congenital heart disease
Venous duplex assessment for varicose veins and reflux
Family history review and cascade screening
redFlags: Recurrent cellulitis of the lymphoedematous limb
Corneal damage or visual compromise from distichiasis
Rapidly progressive or unilateral limb swelling warranting exclusion of secondary cause
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic but generally compatible with a normal lifespan; lymphoedema is manageable with sustained conservative care, and distichiasis is treatable, though recurrent infection, progressive swelling and any associated cardiac disease influence long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Missing distichiasis, which may be subtle and requires careful eyelid examination
Attributing leg swelling to venous disease alone and overlooking the lymphatic diagnosis
Failing to screen for associated congenital heart disease
Not recognising the autosomal dominant inheritance and offering family screening
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
